pages.text:
Saturday number nine started with a hunger that felt like an empty cereal box in my chest. I walked into the kitchen at 7:30 and looked at the counter, then at the family. Dad was still fanning the smoke alarm. Mom was checking her list. Gus was roaring at the toaster.

I asked for pancakes. Fourteen of them.

Dad blinked. "Fourteen? That’s a lot of flour, Max."

"I want whipped cream," I said. "And syrup. And cereal for dessert."

They stared. I have never seen my family stare before. It was like watching a video freeze and then skip to the next level. Dad scrambled the eggs. Mom didn’t say a word. She just wrote "PANCAKES" on her clipboard in big, angry letters.

I ate every bite. It tasted like freedom, which is a word I usually save for when the Wi-Fi works, but today it actually applied. It tasted like sugar and nothing at all.

Then I put on Jonah’s helmet, which I had remembered from the previous Saturday, and I went outside. I found Tessa’s scooter in the garage. I kicked off on Dead Man’s Hill, the long, steep road that ends at the creek. I screamed the whole way down. I didn't care if it sounded like a goose being stepped on. I rode up the hill. I did it again. And again. Thirty-one times over four loops. No bruises. No scraped knees. Just wind and the sound of my own voice getting louder.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy in a red hoodie, rides a small scooter down a steep grassy hill at high speed, mouth wide open in a scream, arms flailing, dust flying behind him, bright midday sun.

pages.text:
Saturdays ten and eleven were about building.

Jonah and I dragged the labeled moving boxes up to the garage roof, cut a hole in the top one, and taped another below it. We had made a slide that went over the fence and straight into Mr. Grady’s inflatable pool, which was bright red and looked like a giant watermelon that had given up on life.

We slid into it. Wet, cold, and laughing, we kept going until our lungs burned.

Then we moved indoors to see how many marshmallows fit in a mouth. Jonah stopped at nineteen, looking proud. I pushed to twenty-seven, which hurt my jaw but didn't kill me.

Mrs. Abernathy arrived at 8:05 with her hot dish. I told her her tomato plants needed a "makeover." We moved them into pots and added mulch. She loved it so much she gave me a tomato the size of a softball.

Then the reset happened. She forgot. I remembered.

I did it again. And again. It was the most fun I had ever had, and it was completely useless.
pages.image: Max and Jonah, both wearing bike helmets, slide down a makeshift cardboard slide into a bright red inflatable pool, water splashing, Mrs. Abernathy in a floral hat watching from the grass with a smile.

pages.text:
Saturday twelve was the day I said everything.

I walked up to Mr. Grady while he was checking his sprinkler and announced that his equipment was a menace, a weapon, and generally hostile to humanity. He looked at me, confused, and said it was just water, son, as if I had accused him of jaywalking.

I pointed at the mailman, who was standing on the wet sidewalk, dripping. "Sir Splashalot," I said. "Nice wet hair."

Then I went to Putt-Putt Palace. I wore my bathrobe. I put a hole-in-one and didn't care. I laughed until my stomach hurt and my eyes watered, the kind of wild, reckless joy that feels like eating the entire sleeve of a candy bar in one go.

No one remembered. No one was angry. No one was hurt.

I was the only one who knew what I had done. And I was the only one who got to keep the laugh.
pages.image: Max, wearing a striped bathrobe over his red hoodie, stands at a mini-golf hole, holding a putter, grinning widely, while Jonah in a bike helmet claps in the background, colorful plastic balls scattered around.

pages.text:
Saturday thirteen was ice cream.

We went to Scoops and I ordered fourteen flavors, one scoop of each: vanilla, chocolate, strawberry, mint chip, rocky road, and the weird one that looked like gravel.

Jonah ate his. I ate mine. It was cold and sweet and heavy, weighing down my tongue like a wet sponge.

"Is this the Golden Age?" Jonah asked, licking the cone.

"I think so," I said.

We sat on the curb watching clouds that were white and puffy and completely unbothered by the move.

Nothing stuck. Nothing cost. I had eaten fourteen flavors of ice cream without a single stomachache, and I had said the rude things without needing to apologize. I had built the slide and left it there, no cleanup required.

It was perfect. It was empty. It felt like holding a soap bubble in your hands; you could feel the surface, but you couldn't keep it.
pages.image: Max and Jonah sit on a concrete curb, holding large ice cream cones with multiple colorful scoops, looking at the sky, a small shop with a striped awning behind them, soft afternoon light.

pages.text:
Saturday fourteen started at 6:47, right on time.

The roar hit my chest. Gus climbed up, his face close and his eyes bright.

"RAAAAWR," he said.

I didn’t get angry. I didn’t feel like popping a zipper. I just felt tired, the kind of tired that stays in your bones even after you sleep.

I had done everything. I had eaten the pancakes. I had slid into the pool. I had said the rude things. I had eaten the ice cream. I had run out of things I wanted.

I lay on the air mattress in the living room. The house was quiet. The boxes were there. The clock was on the wall.

What do you do with a day you can do anything in? You run out of things to do. It’s like playing a video game where you’ve already beaten every level and found every secret, but you still have to press start over and over again.

I closed my eyes. I waited for the next roar. But I knew it wouldn’t come. Not because the day was over, but because I was done.
pages.image: Max lies on a blue air mattress in a living room full of cardboard boxes, eyes closed, looking exhausted, Gus in a green T. rex costume standing nearby, watching him with wide eyes, dim evening light.
